title: Pauri 9: listening, the gods and scriptures
hookLine: suniai: by listening even the lowly speak praise, and the scriptures open (Japji 9)

cards: The uncle who complains through every holiday, every single year. The cynic at work who never has a kind word.
Then something shifts, a loss, a friendship, maybe just time, and one day a generous sentence comes out of that same mouth. The whole table goes quiet. Where did that come from?
This week, pauris nine to fifteen, Japji is about listening and then trusting. And pauri nine, the second listening stanza, has an answer for that uncle.

teach.b: Pauri nine keeps yesterday's drumbeat, suniai, by listening, at the start of every line. In plain words, following Macauliffe: By listening, Shiva, Brahma and Indra.
By listening, even the lowly and the foul-mouthed come to praise. By listening, the ways of yoga and the secrets of the body. By listening, the Shastras, the Smritis and the Vedas.
Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Shiva, Brahma and Indra are great gods in Hindu tradition, and Guru Nanak names them with respect.

The pauri places even their greatness inside listening to the Name. Sikh commentators read it this way: the One is the source, and all greatness, however high, comes by hearing. Then this: suniai mukh saalaahan mand.

teach.h: MAND — EVEN THE BAD MOUTH PRAISES.
teach.b: Mand means the low, the bad; mukh is the mouth. By listening, even those with bad mouths praise. On this reading, nobody is too far gone.
Then the body: jog jugat tan bhed, the methods of yoga and the hidden workings of the body.
Then the scriptures of Guru Nanak's world: Shastras, Smritis, Vedas.
By listening, they open. Their meaning isn't locked in the letters; it comes to the one who listens. Gods, the worst mouth in the room, the body, the books: the pauri says the same thing about each.
Whatever is high, whatever is low, the door is listening.

how: Sikhs recite the ninth pauri each morning as part of Japji's four suniai pauris; each ends with the same refrain, that devotees are always in bloom and listening wipes away pain and wrongdoing.

o: the low, the bad, as in a bad mouth
a temple hymn sung in praise
a high god named beside Indra

games.q: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

s: pauri nine mocks the Hindu gods
it names Shiva, Brahma and Indra with respect, and places their greatness in listening.
by listening, even the foul-mouthed come to praise
the pauri says scriptures open by listening
by listening, the Shastras, Smritis and Vedas.

games.q: pauri nine names the gods, then turns to someone else entirely. who?
o: the lowly and the foul-mouthed, who come to praise.
games.why: suniai mukh saalaahan mand: by listening, even bad mouths turn to praise. nobody is too far gone.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and listen for three sounds: the loudest, then a softer one you'd missed, then the faintest you can find, a hum, a breath, the air itself.

Stay with that third one, and notice how much more you hear when you're looking for it; then imagine hearing, just as freshly, one person whose voice you've stopped listening to. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Mand. The low, the bad: even the bad-mouthed, by listening, come to praise, along with the gods, the body's secrets and the scriptures.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: by listening, even the bad-mouthed praise (Japji, pauri 9).

carryVoice: Your line: the lowly speak praise. Listening can turn even the most bitter tongue. Day one hundred seventy-nine, done.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 9
